extracted.intended_audience: general newspaper readers interested in wartime trials, diplomacy, and postwar organization
extracted.subtask_description: A multi-topic newspaper dispatch covering wartime criminal trials (notably the Yamashita case), appeals and military-legal questions, debates over the site for United Nations headquarters, and diplomatic plans for discussion of atomic energy control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Command responsibility (Yamashita precedent)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Yamashita case is described as 'precedent-setting' — a war leader being tried for war crimes — with debate whether a commander can be held criminally responsible for atrocities committed by his troops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verbatim/close phrasing from page: 'THE YAMASHITA CASE IS PRECEDENT-SETTING ... IT Is ABSURD TO CONSIDER A COMMANDER A MURDERER OR RAPIST BECAUSE ONE OF HIS SOLDIERS COMMITS MURDER OR RAPE ... COMMANDERS MAY BE HELD RESPONSIBLE ... EVEN CRIMINALLY LIABLE, FOR THE LAWLESSNESS OF HIS TROOPS, DEPENDING UPON THE NATURE AND CIRCUMSTANCES SURROUNDING THEM.' Surrounding context: prosecution presented more than 260 witnesses describing widespread atrocities (mass rape, executions, cremation alive), while the general swore he had never heard of them. The passage frames the legal/ethical standard as fact-specific: liability depends on the nature and circumstances of acts by subordinates, and the case is treated as a legal precedent for assessing commander liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals and jurisdictional pathway for military war-crimes trials
rubrics_metrics.description: Description of the sequential avenues of appeal available from a military commission conviction in the Yamashita matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted sequence: 'YAMASHITA'S FIRST APPEAL WILL BE MADE TO LT. GEN. W.D. STYER; ... IF STYER UPHOLDS THE COMMISSION, HE MAY APPEAL TO GENERAL MACARTHUR ... THEN TO THE U.S. SUPREME COURT.' The article notes there may be at least three additional appeals pending and that 'SUPREME COURT TO TAKE JURISDICTION OF HIS CASE' could free him from a military trial. This sets out a procedural rubric: military-commission decision → intermediate military review (e.g., senior general/commissioner) → theater commander (MacArthur) review → possible appeal to U.S. Supreme Court; the availability and effect of each step depends on law and jurisdictional acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria argued for selecting United Nations headquarters site
rubrics_metrics.description: Delegates debated which country should host United Nations headquarters; proponents argued the site must 'fill all the requirements for the world site' and be 'sufficiently detached to survey world problems as a whole.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key quoted rationales: 'Our vote ... goes to San Francisco ... because we feel that it fills all the requirements for the world site.' 'We must have a site sufficiently detached to survey world problems as a whole — a site from which we can get an objective and impartial view.' Other positions noted: some delegates favor Europe or a small country; proponents argued the U.S. is a sanctuary of people of every country and would help public familiarity with international affairs. Practical considerations (cities' ability to host, voting methods, symbolic and accessibility arguments) are presented as criteria for choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of atomic-energy control under international (UN) authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Diplomatic stance and emerging tendency reported that atomic energy (the bomb) should be controlled by an international organization, notably the United Nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page wording: 'decision ... to meet in Moscow on December 15 for discussion of atomic energy controls could be looked upon as a pledge by the major Powers to work together ... members ... believe there is a growing tendency among all nations to favor placing the control of the atomic bomb in the hands of the United Nations Organization.' The article frames this as a policy criterion: atomic energy control should be internationalized (UN oversight) as a necessary step for durable postwar peace; it also notes the subject was expected to dominate the conference agenda and that an exchange of views among the Big Three would be held.
